screens.narratorSegment: Welcome to a pivotal chapter in your Houdini journey! We've learned to create and transform geometry, but to truly harness Houdini's procedural power, we need to understand attributes. Think of attributes as the DNA of your geometry—they are pieces of data attached to every component, from individual points to entire objects. This data allows your models to be dynamic, responsive, and incredibly flexible. In this lesson, we'll demystify what attributes are, how to inspect them, and most importantly, how to programmatically control them using Houdini's high-performance VEX language. Mastering attributes and VEX is the gateway to creating complex, data-driven systems that can generate entire worlds or intricate assets with unprecedented control and efficiency. Get ready to transform your approach to 3D content creation! screens.title: Understanding Geometry Attributes
screens.narratorSegment: At its heart, Houdini's procedural power comes from attributes. Imagine attributes as tiny labels or pieces of data attached to every part of your 3D model. These aren't just decorative; they actively describe and control your geometry. Understanding these different levels is key to knowing where to store and retrieve specific types of information for your procedural effects. content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 2.3›Understanding Attributes

Understanding Geometry Attributes

Data that defines your digital assets.

What are Attributes?

Attributes are pieces of data attached to various components of your geometry. They act as metadata, describing properties like position, color, normal direction, or any custom data you wish to create. They are the core mechanism for dynamic and responsive procedural rules.

Key Takeaway

Attributes are the fundamental data points that drive all procedural effects in Houdini, making geometry dynamic and controllable.

Attribute Component Types

Points

Data attached to individual vertices (e.g., position).

Primitives

Data attached to faces/polygons (e.g., material ID).

Vertices

Data at primitive corners (e.g., UV coordinates).

Detail

Data for the entire geometry (e.g., total area).

screens.title: Key Built-in Attributes in Houdini
screens.narratorSegment: Houdini comes with a rich set of built-in attributes that are automatically generated or utilized by various nodes. Understanding these is fundamental because they represent the most common properties of your geometry. For instance, @P is arguably the most important attribute; it's a vector that stores the X, Y, and Z coordinates of each point, defining its exact location in 3D space. Then we have @Cd, the color attribute, also a vector, which holds the Red, Green, and Blue values for points or vertices. This is how you visually color your geometry. @N represents the normal attribute, a vector indicating the surface direction, crucial for lighting and shading. @uv stores UV texture coordinates, essential for mapping textures onto your models. Finally, @pscale is a float attribute on points, commonly used to control the scale of instances when you're copying geometry. These built-in attributes form the backbone of most procedural operations, allowing you to manipulate fundamental aspects of your models with precision. content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 2.3›Built-in Attributes

Key Built-in Attributes in Houdini

Standard data for position, color, normals, and more.

@P (Position)

A vector (x, y, z) attached to points, defining their location in 3D space. This is fundamental for all geometry.

@Cd (Color)

A vector (red, green, blue) for points or vertices, used to assign visual color to your geometry.

@N (Normal)

A vector (x, y, z) on points or vertices, indicating the surface direction, critical for lighting and shading.

@uv (UV Coordinates)

A vector (u, v) on vertices, used for mapping textures and defining how images wrap around your geometry.

@pscale (Point Scale)

A float attribute on points, commonly used to control the individual scale of instances when copying geometry.

Key Takeaway

Houdini's built-in attributes are the standard language for describing and manipulating geometry, forming the basis of procedural workflows.

screens.title: Using the Attribute Create SOP
screens.narratorSegment: Now that we understand what attributes are and how to inspect them, let's look at how to create them. A simple and direct way to add or modify attributes is by using the Attribute Create SOP. This node is perfect for when you need to define a new attribute and assign a constant value to all components of a specific type, like all points or all primitives. For example, you could use an Attribute Create node to add a new point attribute called 'myCustomValue' and set it to 0.5 for every single point on your geometry. You can specify the attribute's name, its type—such as float, integer, or vector—and then set a uniform value. While incredibly useful for these straightforward, uniform assignments, its capabilities are limited when you need attributes to vary dynamically across your geometry. For more complex, data-driven modifications, we'll need a more powerful tool, which we'll explore next. content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 2.3›Attribute Create SOP

Using the Attribute Create SOP

Adding uniform attributes to your geometry.

Define & Assign Attributes

The Attribute Create SOP allows you to define a new attribute, specify its type (e.g., float, integer, vector), and set a constant value or a simple ramp across your geometry.

  • Choose attribute name and class (point, primitive, etc.).
  • Set data type (float, integer, vector, string).
  • Assign a constant value to all selected components.
Key Takeaway

The Attribute Create SOP is ideal for simple, uniform attribute assignments but lacks the dynamic control of VEX.

Example: Adding a Custom Float Attribute

// Attribute Create SOP Parameters
Attribute Name: myCustomValue
Class: Point
Type: Float
Value: 0.5

// Result in Geometry Spreadsheet (Points tab)
// myCustomValue
// 0.5
// 0.5
// ...
Use Case

Assigning a default 'active' state (e.g., 0 or 1) to all points before further procedural processing.

screens.title: The Attribute Wrangle and VEX Language
screens.narratorSegment: While the Attribute Create SOP is useful for simple tasks, to truly unlock Houdini's procedural potential, we turn to the Attribute Wrangle SOP and the VEX language. VEX, or Vector Expression, is a high-performance, C-like scripting language specifically optimized for parallel processing of geometry data. This means it can efficiently operate on thousands or even millions of points, vertices, or primitives simultaneously, giving you incredibly granular control over your attributes. When you add an Attribute Wrangle node, you'll find a 'VEXpression' editor where you write your code. A critical parameter to understand is 'Run Over,' which determines which component type your VEX code will operate on. If you're modifying point positions, you'll set 'Run Over' to 'Points.' This powerful combination allows you to write short, expressive code snippets that dynamically modify geometry properties based on complex rules, making it indispensable for advanced procedural workflows and game asset generation. content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 2.3›VEX Introduction

The Attribute Wrangle and VEX Language

High-performance scripting for granular control.

What is VEX?

VEX (Vector Expression) is a high-performance, C-like scripting language optimized for parallel processing of geometry data. It allows for granular, programmatic control over attributes.

  • C-like syntax for familiar programming.
  • Optimized for speed and large datasets.
  • Used within the Attribute Wrangle SOP.
Key Takeaway

VEX, accessed via the Attribute Wrangle, is Houdini's most powerful tool for dynamic, data-driven geometry manipulation.

The 'Run Over' Parameter

// Attribute Wrangle SOP
Run Over: Points  // VEX code operates on each point
Run Over: Primitives // VEX code operates on each primitive
Run Over: Vertices // VEX code operates on each vertex
Run Over: Detail   // VEX code operates once on the entire geometry
Important Note

Always match the 'Run Over' setting to the component type of the attribute you intend to modify (e.g., '@P' for 'Points').

screens.title: Coloring Geometry with VEX
screens.narratorSegment: Let's dive into our first practical VEX examples, focusing on modifying the color attribute, @Cd. To set all points of a geometry to a uniform green, you would use a simple assignment: @Cd equals open curly brace 0, 1, 0 close curly brace.. Here, open curly brace 0, 1, 0 close curly brace represents an RGB vector where Red is 0, Green is 1, and Blue is 0. This is a quick way to apply a solid color. For something more dynamic, we can create a color gradient based on the point number, @ptnum. The expression @Cd equals open curly brace @ptnum slash open parenthesis float open parenthesis npoints open parenthesis 0 close parenthesis close parenthesis - 1 close parenthesis, 0, 0 close curly brace. creates a red gradient. @ptnum is the unique index of each point, and npoints open parenthesis 0 close parenthesis returns the total number of points in the first input. We cast npoints open parenthesis 0 close parenthesis to a float to ensure floating-point division, otherwise, integer division would truncate the result to zero, which is a common mistake. This example demonstrates how VEX allows you to create visually rich effects by linking attributes to procedural data.

content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 2.3›VEX Color Example

Coloring Geometry with VEX

Applying uniform and gradient colors.

Uniform Color Assignment

Set all points to a specific color by assigning a constant vector to the @Cd attribute. Remember to set 'Run Over' to 'Points'.

@Cd = {0, 1, 0}; // Set RGB to green

Gradient Color based on Point Number

Create a dynamic color gradient using @ptnum (point index) and npoints(0) (total points).

@Cd = { @ptnum / (float(npoints(0)) - 1), 0, 0 }; // Red gradient
Key Takeaway

VEX allows you to precisely control color attributes, from simple uniform assignments to complex gradients driven by geometry data.

VEX Variables Explained
  • @Cd: The color attribute (vector).
  • @ptnum: The current point's unique index.
  • npoints(0): Total points in the first input.
  • float(): Casts an integer to a float for accurate division.
Common Mistake

Forgetting to cast integers to floats in division (e.g., 1/2 results in 0, not 0.5). Always use float() for decimal results.

screens.title: Deforming Geometry with VEX
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond just coloring, VEX truly shines when you want to dynamically deform your geometry. Let's explore how to modify the position attribute, @P, to create a wave deformation on a flat grid. The VEX expression @P. y plus equals sin open parenthesis @P. x asterisk 5 close parenthesis asterisk 0.1. displaces points in the Y-axis based on their X-position. Here, @P. y accesses the Y component of the point's position, and @P. x accesses its X component. The sin open parenthesis close parenthesis function creates a smooth, oscillating wave pattern. Multiplying @P. x by 5 controls the frequency of the wave, making it more compressed or stretched, while multiplying the entire sine result by 0.1 scales the amplitude, determining how tall or short the wave will be. This example demonstrates how you can use mathematical functions within VEX to create complex, organic deformations that would be incredibly difficult to achieve manually. Remember to set the Attribute Wrangle's 'Run Over' parameter to 'Points' since we are directly manipulating point positions. content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 2.3›VEX Position Example

Deforming Geometry with VEX

Creating wave effects using point positions.

Wave Deformation on a Grid

Displace points in the Y-axis based on their X-position using a sine wave. This creates a dynamic, undulating surface.

@P.y += sin(@P.x * 5) * 0.1; // Displace points in Y
Key Takeaway

Manipulating the @P attribute with mathematical functions in VEX enables powerful and complex geometric deformations.

VEX Components Explained
  • @P.y: Y-component of the point's position.
  • @P.x: X-component of the point's position.
  • sin(): Trigonometric sine function for wave patterns.
  • * 5: Controls the frequency of the wave.
  • * 0.1: Controls the amplitude (height) of the wave.
Real-world Connection

This technique is used to create realistic water surfaces, cloth simulations, or organic terrain deformations in games and visual effects.

screens.title: Randomizing Scale for Instances with VEX
screens.narratorSegment: Another powerful application of VEX is controlling the scale of instances when copying geometry. When you use a 'Copy to Points' node, it looks for a special attribute called @pscale on the points to determine the size of each copied instance. If @pscale isn't present, all copies will be the same size. To give each point a unique, random scale, you can use the VEX expression @pscale equals rand open parenthesis @ptnum close parenthesis.. Here, rand open parenthesis close parenthesis is a VEX function that generates a pseudo-random float value between 0 and 1. By feeding @ptnum, the current point's unique index, as the seed to rand open parenthesis close parenthesis, we ensure that each point receives a different random value. This results in varied scales for your copied geometry, which is incredibly useful for creating natural-looking scatter systems like foliage, rocks, or debris in game environments. This simple line of VEX unlocks a world of organic variation and visual richness in your procedural assets. keyIdea.title: Randomized Instancing
keyIdea.text: VEX enables randomized scaling of instances via the @pscale attribute and the rand() function, creating natural variations in copied geometry.

content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 2.3›VEX Pscale Example

Randomizing Scale for Instances with VEX

Using @pscale and rand() for varied copies.

Controlling Instance Scale

The @pscale attribute on points controls the individual scale of geometry copied onto those points. Without it, all copies are uniform.

@pscale = rand(@ptnum); // Random scale for each point
Key Takeaway

@pscale combined with rand(@ptnum) is essential for creating natural, varied instancing effects in procedural environments.

VEX Functions Explained
  • @pscale: The point scale attribute (float).
  • rand(): Generates a pseudo-random float between 0 and 1.
  • @ptnum: Used as a unique seed for rand() per point.
Pro Tip

To get a random scale within a specific range (e.g., 0.5 to 1.5), you can modify the expression: @pscale = rand(@ptnum) * 1.0 + 0.5;

screens.title: Troubleshooting VEX Expressions
screens.narratorSegment: As you start writing more VEX, you'll inevitably encounter errors. Knowing the common pitfalls can save you a lot of time. First, always remember your semicolons! Like C-style languages, every VEX statement must end with a semicolon. Forgetting this is a frequent cause of syntax errors. Second, ensure your 'Run Over' parameter matches the attribute type you're targeting. Trying to access @P while running over 'Primitives' won't work correctly, as @P is a point attribute. Third, be mindful of type mismatches; don't try to assign a vector to a float attribute without proper conversion. A classic mistake is integer division: 1 slash 2 in VEX results in 0, not 0.5. Always cast integers to floats, like float open parenthesis npoints open parenthesis 0 close parenthesis close parenthesis, when you need decimal results. Finally, for debugging, learn to read the errors in the console, and don't hesitate to use print f open parenthesis close parenthesis statements within your VEX code, similar to print open parenthesis close parenthesis in Python, to output values and track your logic. These practices will make your VEX journey much smoother.

content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 2.3›VEX Troubleshooting

Troubleshooting VEX Expressions

Understanding common errors and debugging techniques.

Common VEX Mistakes

  • Missing Semicolons: Every VEX statement must end with ;.
  • Incorrect 'Run Over': Ensure it matches the attribute type you're modifying.
  • Type Mismatches: Assigning a vector to a float or vice-versa without conversion.
  • Integer Division: 1/2 results in 0. Use float() for decimal results.
Key Takeaway

Proactive awareness of common VEX errors and utilizing debugging tools like printf() are crucial for efficient procedural development.

Debugging with printf()

Use printf() statements within your VEX code to output values to the console, similar to print() in Python. This helps track variable states and logic flow.

// Example: Debugging @P.x value
printf("Point %d X position: %f
", @ptnum, @P.x);

// This will print to the console for each point:
// Point 0 X position: -0.500000
// Point 1 X position: 0.000000
// ...
Pro Tip

Always check the Houdini console for VEX error messages; they often provide clues to the exact line and type of error.
